title: Ki Tavo: a wandering Aramean (Deuteronomy 26:5)
hook: "A wandering Aramean was my father", now at the heart of the Passover Haggadah

segments.voice: Yesterday, bikkurim, the first fruits in a basket. Your line was the first goes to thanks. What was your first, and where did it go? Today, the story the farmer tells as he sets the basket down. Day five hundred thirteen.

At the Passover seder, the Haggadah reaches a long stretch of verses and commentary, the telling of the Exodus itself. Look closely at the verses it's built on, and they aren't from the book of Exodus. They're from Deuteronomy, from the speech of the farmer with his basket. The Haggadah takes his few lines and reads them slowly, phrase by phrase, as the backbone of the night's story. And it starts with a phrase readers still argue over.
screen: `THE SEDER TABLE.` → `NOT EXODUS: DEUTERONOMY.` → `THE FARMER'S SPEECH.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, the speech begins: "A wandering Aramean was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there, few in number; and he became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous." In Hebrew, arami oved avi. Three words, and readers don't agree on what they say. Oved can mean wandering, lost, or perishing. Commentators like Ibn Ezra and Rashbam read it plainly: my ancestor, Jacob, or perhaps Abraham, was a wandering Aramean, a man without land of his own. The Haggadah, and Rashi after it, read it another way: an Aramean, Laban, tried to destroy my father Jacob. Two readings, both kept. One says, we came from wanderers. The other says, we came through danger. Now notice what the farmer is doing. He's standing with his own harvest, settled at last, and the first thing out of his mouth is: we were not always settled. My people were strangers once. And he says my father, not their father. It's personal. The Mishnah asks the same of everyone at the seder: begin with the shame and end with the praise, and tell it as your own story. Settled people are asked to remember, out loud, that they weren't always. The Torah ties that memory to its law: love the stranger, it says elsewhere, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. One line of family history, and a rule for how to treat the newcomer next door.
screen: `ARAMI OVED AVI.` · `WANDERING, OR PERISHING?` · `TWO READINGS, BOTH KEPT.` · `MY FATHER, NOT THEIR FATHER.` · then, large: `A WANDERING FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell your family's story in one line. Settle, and breathe. Go back as far as you know. A grandparent, a great-grandmother, a name on an old document, or just a guess. Where did they come from? What did they carry, or leave behind? Now try to say it in one sentence, the way the farmer does. Something like: my grandmother crossed an ocean with one suitcase. If you don't know your family's story, that not-knowing is part of many families' story too. Hold the line you've found, and let it sit. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. The portion that begins with arriving, and asks you to remember wandering.
Your line: a wandering father. Today, tell someone one line of your family's story, or ask someone for theirs. Day five hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Deuteronomy 26:5–8 is the core text of the Maggid section of the Passover Haggadah, where it is read and expounded phrase by phrase, opening with the Haggadah's reading of 'arami oved avi'.

fork.setup: you're the farmer, settled, your harvest in a basket at the altar. what's the first thing the Torah has you say?
options: a story: my father was a wandering Aramean.
a request for next year's rain.
fork.reveal: before any thanks for the harvest, he tells where his people came from: wanderers, then slaves, then rescued.

original.note: Hebrew: a wandering Aramean was my father, or, as the Haggadah reads it, an Aramean sought to destroy my father.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about someone's ancient ancestor.
what it means: the settled farmer remembers out loud that his people were once wanderers and strangers.
what a scholar hears: the Haggadah and Rashi read oved as 'sought to destroy' (Laban against Jacob); Ibn Ezra and Rashbam read it as a homeless, wandering ancestor.

notes: Deuteronomy 26:5 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify wording and punctuation.
Ibn Ezra reads the Aramean as Jacob, poor and wandering; Rashbam reads it as Abraham wandering from Aram. Confirm attributions.
Mishnah Pesachim 10:4: begin with disgrace and end with praise, and expound 'arami oved avi' to the end of the passage; 'tell it as your own story' leans also on Pesachim 10:5. Paraphrased.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the hook said the seder's verses 'aren't from Exodus at all', but the Haggadah's midrash quotes Exodus verses too; it now says the verses the telling is built on come from Deuteronomy. Cut 'for two thousand years' and the hook's claim that attention drifts. The teach's closing uplift line replaced with the paraphrased link to Deuteronomy 10:19 (added to sources).
